newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: ALPINE SKIING-SYKORA SURVIVES NEAR-CRASHES TO WIN SLALOM.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SYKORA SURVIVES NEAR-CRASHES TO WIN SLALOM.

text.p: In-form Austrian Thomas Sykora was overjoyed at surviving a bumpy piste and several near-crashes to win his third World Cup slalom of the season on Monday.
"I am really freaked out about myself," Sykora said. "I can make as many mistakes as I want and still always be in front. It's incredible and I just don't understand.
"This season I have been unable to produce two clean runs in a race and yet I still win."

Despite almost crashing out in the second run because of a poor piste and bad visibility, Sykora still managed to clock a winning aggregate time of one minute 41.93 seconds, ahead of Frenchman Sebastien Amiez and fellow Austrian Thomas Stangassinger
The 28-year-old Sykora has won three of the four slaloms staged so far this winter and finished second in the other, to take a commanding lead in the discipline's standings with 380 points.
"The conditions were extremely demanding today. It was foggy and the snow was too soft," said Sykora, adding that the second leg should have been run in reverse-15 order instead of reverse-30.
"But I tried not to think about the difficulties. I just continued pushing myself down after every mistake and never stopped throwing myself into the gates.
"To win in perfect conditions is great but to win in poor conditions is even more satisfying. This is one of my greatest wins," said Sykora, who now has five career World Cup victories.
Sykora established himself on the circuit last winter after beating Italian Alberto Tomba on the prestigious and classic course in Kitzbuehel for his maiden victory.
"Something changed in my mind after that victory. Suddenly I realised I could always be in the top three if I really wanted to," said Sykora.
Tomba himself finished only eighth on Monday and was furious at the official decision to let the top 30 from the first leg race in reverse order in the second run.
World Cup rules allow for the second leg to start with the top 15 in poor conditions, to save the course from breaking up too much for the better skiers.

"It was ridiculous to have the reverse-30 rule," the world slalom champion said. "I train alone and can't make such big holes in my own specially prepared slope so it is impossible for me to train in such conditions."
"This gives me another reason to doubt my future in ski racing," said Tomba, who has been speculating aloud about retiring since the 1996 world championships in Sierra Nevada.
Amiez, the defending slalom World Cup title-holder, was content with second place on the Podkoren slope in 1:42.29 for his best result of the season.

"I put too much pressure on myself at the beginning of the season and therefore had a bad start. But I am constantly improving," said Amiez, whose only other podium finish this winter was third in Madonna di Campiglio in December.
"It's a good omen for the next slalom in Chamonix (January 12) which was where I earned my first top 10 result in 1994," said the 24-year-old Frenchman.
Stangassinger, the 1994 Olympic slalom champion, fell back to overall third in 1:42.34 after a first-descent lead, and said: "I must be pleased, I haven't posted a fastest first run in a long time."
The biggest surprise of the day was Matt Grosjean's fourth place in 1:42.49 -- the best result by an American in slalom since Felix MacGrath was second in Aare, Sweden, in 1988.
"I have to continue dreaming about my first podium finish but I am getting closer," said Grosjean. "I blew my podium chances in the first run with a big mistake."
The men's World Cup circuit moves to Chamonix, France, on January 11 and 12 for a downhill, slalom and the first combined event of the winter.
